meta.name: First aid
meta.about: First aid and emergency guidance written to follow the Resuscitation Council UK 2021 guidelines, the European Resuscitation Council, the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation consensus, and NHS and St John Ambulance public advice. It is educational and no substitute for a certified first-aid course. 'Emergency services' means 999 in the UK, 112 across Europe and 911 in North America.

cpr.name: CPR and using a defibrillator
cpr.summary: When the heart stops, blood stops reaching the brain and brain cells begin to die within minutes. Chest compressions squeeze the heart between the sternum and spine to keep some blood moving; a defibrillator can restart a heart that is quivering (fibrillating) rather than pumping. Starting CPR at once and using an AED within minutes can double or triple survival.
recognise: Collapsed, unresponsive to shouting and shaking the shoulders
Not breathing, or only gasping (agonal gasps are not normal breathing)
Do not waste time feeling for a pulse

steps.title: Check safety and response
steps.detail: Make sure the scene is safe. Shout and gently shake the shoulders. If there is no response, shout for help.

steps.title: Open the airway and check breathing
steps.detail: Tilt the head back and lift the chin. Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.

steps.title: Call emergency services
steps.detail: If not breathing normally, call 999/112 on speaker so your hands are free, and send someone for a public-access defibrillator (AED).

steps.title: Start chest compressions
steps.detail: Kneel beside the person. Put the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the sternum) and the other hand on top, arms straight. Press down 5-6 cm at 100-120 per minute (the beat of 'Stayin' Alive'), letting the chest recoil fully each time.

steps.title: Give rescue breaths if trained and willing
steps.detail: After 30 compressions, tilt the head, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs and blow steadily for 1 second until the chest rises; give 2 breaths, then 30 more compressions. If unable or unwilling, give continuous compressions only.

steps.title: Use the AED as soon as it arrives
steps.detail: Turn it on and follow the voice prompts. Attach the pads to bare skin: one below the right collarbone, one on the left side below the armpit. Let it analyse (nobody touching), press the shock button if told, then immediately resume compressions.

steps.title: Keep going
steps.detail: Continue 30:2 (or continuous compressions), swapping rescuers every 2 minutes to avoid tiring, until the person shows signs of life, professionals take over, or you are exhausted. If they start breathing normally, place them in the recovery position and keep watching.

cpr.children: Children and infants: give 5 initial rescue breaths, then 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Compress a third of the chest depth: one hand for a child, two fingers or two thumbs for an infant. If alone, do a minute of CPR before calling.
dont: Do not delay compressions to look for a pulse or to fetch equipment yourself
Do not stop compressions for more than 10 seconds at a time
Do not be afraid of doing harm: ribs may crack, but no CPR is far worse
Do not remove AED pads or turn it off once attached
callFor: Always: any unresponsive person who is not breathing normally is a cardiac arrest until proven otherwise
cpr.why: The heart lies behind the lower sternum, and compressing 5-6 cm squeezes blood out through the aortic and pulmonary valves; recoil refills it. Rescue breaths keep some oxygen entering the lungs, but the blood already holds several minutes' supply, which is why compression-only CPR works for bystanders. Ventricular fibrillation, the commonest rhythm at collapse, is a chaotic electrical storm that only a shock can reset, and every minute without a shock cuts survival by about 10%.

references.title: Resuscitation Council UK: Adult basic life support guidelines 2021

heart-attack.name: Heart attack
heart-attack.summary: A coronary artery has blocked and heart muscle is dying. Survival and the amount of muscle saved depend on how fast the artery is reopened, so the first-aid job is recognition and a fast call, keeping the person still and calm, and being ready to start CPR.
recognise: Central chest pain or pressure, like a tight band or heavy weight, lasting more than 15 minutes
Pain spreading to the arms (usually left), jaw, neck or back
Sweating, grey or pale skin, nausea, breathlessness, light-headedness
Women, older people and people with diabetes more often have breathlessness, indigestion-like discomfort or extreme tiredness without classic pain

steps.title: Call emergency services immediately
steps.detail: Say you suspect a heart attack. Do not drive them to hospital yourself unless there is no ambulance service: an ambulance brings a defibrillator and can start treatment and alert the catheter lab.

steps.title: Sit them down and keep them still
steps.detail: A half-sitting position with knees bent and back supported (the 'W' position) eases the heart's work. Loosen tight clothing. Reassure them.

steps.title: Give aspirin if available and not allergic
steps.detail: One 300 mg tablet chewed slowly (or 4 x 75 mg). It begins to stop platelets clumping in the blocked artery. Do not give it if they are allergic or have been told not to take aspirin.

steps.title: Help with their own GTN spray
steps.detail: If they have angina medication, help them take it as prescribed.

steps.title: Watch and be ready
steps.detail: Stay with them. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR and send for a defibrillator.

dont: Do not let them walk about, eat, or 'see if it passes'
Do not give aspirin to someone with a known allergy or bleeding problem, or to children
Do not leave them alone
callFor: Chest pain or discomfort lasting more than 15 minutes, or shorter but with breathlessness, sweating, collapse or a known heart condition
heart-attack.why: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve and run across the heart's surface. A ruptured plaque in one of them triggers a clot that blocks flow; muscle downstream is ischaemic within seconds and starts dying within 20-30 minutes. Chewed aspirin reaches platelets within minutes; angioplasty within 90-120 minutes of the call saves the most muscle.

references.title: British Heart Foundation: Heart attack symptoms

stroke.name: Stroke: recognise and act FAST
stroke.summary: A blood vessel in the brain has blocked or burst. Around two million neurons die every minute the blockage persists, but clot-busting drugs and clot retrieval can reverse the damage if given within hours. There is nothing to do at the scene except recognise it and get an ambulance.
recognise: Face: has it drooped on one side? Can they smile?
Arms: can they raise both arms and keep them there?
Speech: is it slurred, garbled or absent? Can they understand you?
Time: call emergency services at once if any of these are present
Also: sudden loss of vision, sudden severe headache, sudden numbness or weakness down one side, sudden confusion, loss of balance or a fall

steps.title: Call emergency services
steps.detail: Say the word 'stroke' and the time the symptoms started (or when they were last seen well). The time decides which treatments are possible.

steps.title: Keep them safe and comfortable
steps.detail: Help them lie down with head and shoulders slightly raised, or on their side if drowsy or vomiting. Loosen tight clothing.

steps.title: Give nothing to eat or drink
steps.detail: Swallowing is often impaired and fluid can enter the lungs; they may need surgery or anaesthesia.

steps.title: Reassure and monitor
steps.detail: Talk calmly even if they cannot reply. Note the time and any changes. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR.

dont: Do not give aspirin: a bleeding stroke looks identical and aspirin would worsen it
Do not let them 'sleep it off' or wait for symptoms to pass, even if they improve (a transient ischaemic attack is a warning of an imminent stroke)
Do not give food, drink or their usual tablets
callFor: Any FAST sign, however brief, even if it has resolved
stroke.why: The middle cerebral artery supplies the face, arm and speech areas of the cortex, which is why FAST catches most strokes. Neurons deprived of oxygenated blood stop firing in seconds and die in minutes, but the surrounding 'penumbra' survives for hours on collateral flow and is what treatment saves. A thrombectomy retrieves the clot through a catheter from the femoral artery up to the brain.

choking.name: Choking
choking.summary: Food or an object has lodged in the larynx or trachea. If the person can still cough, their own cough is the best tool; if they cannot breathe, cough or speak, back blows and abdominal thrusts create bursts of pressure to expel the object, and if they collapse, chest compressions do the same job.
recognise: Sudden inability to speak, clutching the throat, usually while eating
Mild: can cough forcefully, speak, breathe
Severe: cannot speak or cough effectively, silent attempts to breathe, high-pitched noises, face turning blue, then unconsciousness

steps.title: Mild obstruction: encourage coughing
steps.detail: Stay with them and encourage them to keep coughing. Do nothing else unless it becomes severe.

steps.title: Severe: give up to 5 back blows
steps.detail: Stand to the side and slightly behind. Support their chest with one hand and lean them forward. Give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking after each whether the obstruction has cleared.

steps.title: Then up to 5 abdominal thrusts
steps.detail: Stand behind them, put both arms round the upper abdomen, lean them forward. Make a fist and place it between the navel and the bottom of the sternum; grasp it with the other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards. Repeat up to 5 times.

steps.title: Alternate and call for help
steps.detail: Continue alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. If not already done, call emergency services (or have someone call) once the first cycle fails.

steps.title: If they become unconscious
steps.detail: Lower them to the ground, call emergency services, and start CPR beginning with chest compressions. Look in the mouth before rescue breaths and remove anything visible; do not sweep blindly with a finger.

choking.children: Infants under 1: lay face down along your forearm with the head low, give 5 back blows; then turn face up and give 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower sternum. Never use abdominal thrusts on an infant. Children over 1: as for adults, with less force.
dont: Do not slap the back of someone who is coughing effectively
Do not use abdominal thrusts on infants or in late pregnancy (use chest thrusts instead)
Do not finger-sweep blindly: it can push the object deeper
callFor: Any severe choking
Anyone who received abdominal thrusts should be medically checked afterwards, as they can injure internal organs
choking.why: The larynx is the narrowest point of the adult airway and the epiglottis normally seals it during swallowing; talking or laughing while eating lets food slip past. A back blow or abdominal thrust suddenly raises pressure in the chest, forcing the air trapped in the lungs up the trachea like a cork from a bottle.

references.title: NHS: What to do if someone is choking

severe-bleeding.name: Severe bleeding
severe-bleeding.summary: An adult has about 5 litres of blood and can lose a fifth before the body's compensation fails; a severed artery can do that in minutes. Direct pressure on the wound is the single most effective measure, with a tourniquet for limb bleeding that pressure cannot control.
recognise: Blood soaking through clothing or dressings, pooling, or spurting (arterial)
Signs of shock as blood is lost: pale, cold, clammy skin, fast breathing, rapid weak pulse, thirst, confusion, then collapse
Amputations and deep wounds of the neck, armpit or groin bleed catastrophically

steps.title: Protect yourself and call
steps.detail: Wear gloves if available. Call emergency services or have someone call while you act.

steps.title: Apply firm direct pressure
steps.detail: Press hard on the wound with a pad, clean cloth or your hands, directly over the bleeding point. Do not lift it to look. If blood soaks through, add more on top and press harder.

steps.title: Pack deep wounds
steps.detail: For a deep wound in the neck, armpit or groin where a tourniquet cannot go, pack gauze or clean cloth tightly into the wound and keep pressing.

steps.title: Apply a tourniquet if a limb keeps bleeding
steps.detail: If direct pressure fails for a limb, or the bleeding is catastrophic, place a tourniquet (commercial, or improvised from a wide band and a stick to twist) 5-7 cm above the wound, not over a joint, and tighten until bleeding stops. Note the time. Do not loosen it.

steps.title: Treat for shock
steps.detail: Lie them down, raise the legs if injuries allow, keep them warm, and do not give food or drink. Keep pressing on the wound until help arrives.

steps.title: If they become unresponsive
steps.detail: Check breathing; start CPR if not breathing normally.

dont: Do not remove a large embedded object: press around it instead
Do not release pressure to check or change dressings
Do not apply a tourniquet loosely or over a joint, and never remove one before medical care
Do not give anything to drink
callFor: Any bleeding that soaks through a dressing, spurts, or comes from a deep or large wound
Any wound with signs of shock, or in someone on blood thinners
severe-bleeding.why: Pressure closes the vessel against underlying tissue and lets a clot form; arteries have muscular walls that contract but keep pumping at systolic pressure, so only sustained force stops them. A tourniquet compresses the artery against bone: the femoral and brachial arteries lie close to the femur and humerus, which is why limb tourniquets work. Shock is the failure to deliver oxygen once blood volume falls; the body diverts blood from skin (pale, cold) and speeds the heart to compensate.

references.title: NHS: How to treat severe bleeding

burns.name: Burns and scalds
burns.summary: Heat keeps damaging skin for minutes after the source is removed, so cooling with running water is the treatment that changes outcomes. The depth and area of a burn decide what happens next: superficial burns heal in a week, deep ones need grafts, and large burns lose fluid fast enough to cause shock.
recognise: Superficial: red, painful, dry, like sunburn
Partial thickness: blisters, weeping, very painful, red or mottled
Full thickness: white, leathery or charred, may be painless because nerve endings are destroyed
Size: the person's palm is about 1% of their body surface

steps.title: Stop the burning
steps.detail: Remove the person from the heat. Put out flames: stop, drop and roll, or smother with a blanket. For chemicals, brush off powder and flood with water; for electrical burns, switch off the supply first.

steps.title: Cool with running water for 20 minutes
steps.detail: Cool tap water (not ice) over the burn as soon as possible, and still worthwhile within 3 hours of the injury. Keep the rest of the person warm to avoid hypothermia, especially children.

steps.title: Remove clothing and jewellery
steps.detail: Take off anything near the burn before swelling starts, unless it is stuck to the skin.

steps.title: Cover loosely
steps.detail: After cooling, cover with cling film laid on (not wrapped around) or a clean, non-fluffy cloth or plastic bag for a hand or foot. This reduces pain and infection risk.

steps.title: Relieve pain and seek assessment
steps.detail: Paracetamol or ibuprofen. Sit upright for facial burns and burns from inhaled smoke.

dont: Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste, creams or oils
Do not burst blisters
Do not remove stuck clothing
Do not use adhesive dressings or fluffy material on the burn
callFor: All chemical and electrical burns
Burns larger than the person's hand, deep burns, or any burn to the face, hands, feet, genitals or across a joint
Burns with breathing difficulty, soot around the nose or mouth, or from an enclosed fire
Burns in children under 5, the elderly, pregnant women, or anyone with signs of shock
burns.why: Skin is the barrier against fluid loss and infection, and its dermis holds the nerve endings and the sweat glands and hair follicles from which new skin regrows. Cooling draws heat out of the tissue and halts the zone of ongoing damage around the burn; a burn that destroys the dermis cannot regrow skin from within and must be grafted. Large burns leak plasma into the tissue, causing hypovolaemic shock over hours.

fractures.name: Fractures and dislocations
fractures.summary: A broken bone is rarely life-threatening in itself, but the sharp ends can cut vessels and nerves, and the femur and pelvis can bleed litres into surrounding tissue. First aid means keeping the limb still in the position found, controlling bleeding, and getting the person to imaging without making things worse.
recognise: Pain, swelling and bruising over a bone after injury
Deformity, shortening or an unnatural angle; a grating sensation
Inability to bear weight or use the limb
Open fracture: bone visible or a wound over the break
Dislocation: a joint out of shape, locked, with intense pain (shoulders, fingers, kneecaps most often)

steps.title: Keep the injured part still
steps.detail: Tell them not to move it. Support it in the position found with your hands, rolled clothing or cushions. Do not try to straighten it.

steps.title: Control bleeding and cover open wounds
steps.detail: Apply pressure around, not on, protruding bone. Cover the wound with a clean dressing.

steps.title: Immobilise for transport
steps.detail: For an arm, a sling or securing it to the body; for a leg, padding between the legs and broad bandages tying it to the uninjured leg above and below the break, not over it. Splint only if trained and the person must be moved.

steps.title: Check circulation beyond the injury
steps.detail: Colour, warmth and sensation in the fingers or toes before and after immobilising; loosen bandages if they become pale, cold or numb.

steps.title: Cool, comfort and go to hospital
steps.detail: Ice wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes reduces swelling. Nothing to eat or drink in case surgery is needed. Call an ambulance for legs, hips, pelvis, spine or if they cannot be moved safely.

dont: Do not try to push a dislocated joint back or straighten a deformed limb
Do not move someone with a suspected spinal, hip or pelvic injury unless in immediate danger
Do not give food or drink
Do not let them walk on a suspected leg fracture
callFor: Suspected fractures of the thigh, hip, pelvis or spine, or any open fracture
A limb that is pale, cold, numb or pulseless beyond the injury
Head, neck or back injury, or an injury from a major mechanism (fall from height, road collision)
Signs of shock
fractures.why: Bone is stiff and fails suddenly under bending or twisting loads; the periosteum and marrow are richly supplied with blood, so every fracture bleeds. The femoral shaft can hide 1-1.5 litres and a pelvic fracture more. Keeping the ends still limits bleeding, pain and further damage to the nerves and arteries that run alongside every long bone (the radial nerve on the humerus, the popliteal artery behind the knee). Healing begins with a haematoma that becomes soft callus in weeks and hard bone in months.

sprains.name: Sprains and strains
sprains.summary: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament (the bands that hold a joint together); a strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon. Most heal with protection, early gentle movement and time. The first days aim to limit swelling and pain, the following weeks to restore movement and strength.
recognise: Pain, swelling and bruising around a joint (sprain) or in a muscle belly (strain) after a twist, fall or sudden effort
Difficulty putting weight through the joint or using the muscle
A 'pop' at the time of injury with rapid swelling suggests a more serious ligament tear
Suspect a fracture instead if there is bony tenderness, deformity, or inability to take four steps

steps.title: Protect
steps.detail: Stop the activity. Support the limb; use crutches or a brace for a day or two if weight-bearing is painful.

steps.title: Rest, then load gradually
steps.detail: Rest for the first 24-72 hours, then begin gentle movement and progressive weight-bearing: complete rest slows recovery.

steps.title: Ice
steps.detail: An ice pack wrapped in a towel for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours during the first 2-3 days, for pain relief.

steps.title: Compression
steps.detail: An elastic bandage snug but not tight, removed at night, to limit swelling.

steps.title: Elevation
steps.detail: Raise the limb above heart level when resting.

steps.title: Pain relief and rehabilitation
steps.detail: Paracetamol or ibuprofen; once pain allows, range-of-motion, balance and strengthening exercises to prevent re-injury. Most ankle sprains improve in 2 weeks and heal in 6-12.

dont: Do not apply ice directly to skin or for more than 20 minutes
Do not apply heat, drink alcohol, run or massage in the first 72 hours (they increase bleeding and swelling)
Do not immobilise for weeks: stiffness and weakness follow
callFor: Seek urgent care if the joint looks deformed, you heard a crack, cannot bear weight at all, or numbness or pale cold skin develops
See a clinician if it is no better after a week, or the joint gives way repeatedly
sprains.why: Ligaments are dense collagen with a poor blood supply, so they heal slowly and by scar; the lateral ankle ligaments tear when the foot rolls inward, the knee's cruciate and collateral ligaments with twisting. Ice numbs pain nerves and slows local bleeding; elevation and compression use gravity and pressure to limit fluid leaking from damaged capillaries. Controlled loading aligns the new collagen fibres along lines of stress, which is why early movement gives stronger healing than rest.

fainting.name: Fainting
fainting.summary: A faint is a brief loss of consciousness because blood pressure drops and the brain is starved of blood for a few seconds. Lying flat restores flow and recovery is quick; the first-aid task is to protect the person from injury, check they are breathing, and recognise the collapses that are not simple faints.
recognise: Warning: light-headed, pale, sweaty, nauseous, vision greying or tunnelling, ringing ears
Triggers: standing for long periods, heat, pain, the sight of blood, fear, standing up quickly, dehydration, missed meals
Brief loss of consciousness (seconds to a minute) with full recovery within minutes; a few jerks can occur
Not a simple faint if: it happened during exercise, with chest pain or palpitations, lying down, with a seizure lasting minutes, injury, slow recovery, or in someone with heart disease

steps.title: If they feel faint
steps.detail: Help them lie down and raise their legs on a chair or your shoulders. If they cannot lie down, sit with head between knees. Loosen tight clothing, fresh air.

steps.title: If they have fainted
steps.detail: Check they are breathing normally. Raise their legs above heart level. They should come round within a minute or two.

steps.title: Recovery position if unconscious but breathing
steps.detail: Kneel beside them; place the near arm at a right angle, bring the far hand against the near cheek, bend the far knee and roll them towards you onto their side, head tilted back so the airway stays open and any vomit drains. Keep checking breathing.

steps.title: Afterwards
steps.detail: Keep them lying for 10-15 minutes, then sit up slowly. Offer water once fully alert. Look for injuries from the fall.

steps.title: If they are not breathing normally
steps.detail: Call emergency services and start CPR.

dont: Do not sit or stand them up straight away
Do not give food or drink until fully awake
Do not leave an unconscious person on their back
Do not splash water or slap them
callFor: Not breathing normally, or unresponsive for more than a minute or two
Injury from the fall, especially to the head
Fainting during exercise, with chest pain or palpitations, in pregnancy, or in someone with diabetes or heart disease
Repeated faints, or a first faint in an older adult
fainting.why: Standing pools half a litre of blood in the leg veins; normally baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect the pressure drop and the brainstem speeds the heart and constricts vessels within a beat. In a vasovagal faint the reflex misfires: the vagus nerve slows the heart and vessels dilate, cerebral perfusion falls below the threshold needed to stay conscious, and the person falls. Lying flat removes the gravity gradient and the brain refills within seconds.

seizures.name: Seizures
seizures.summary: A seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Most stop by themselves within a couple of minutes and the person needs protection from injury, not restraint. A seizure that lasts more than 5 minutes, or repeats without recovery, is a medical emergency.
recognise: Tonic-clonic: sudden stiffening and collapse, then rhythmic jerking of limbs, possibly a cry, blue lips, frothing, tongue biting, incontinence; drowsiness and confusion afterwards
Focal or absence seizures: staring, lip smacking, fumbling, unresponsiveness for seconds to minutes without falling
Febrile convulsion: a seizure in a young child with a high temperature

steps.title: Protect from harm
steps.detail: Note the time. Clear hard or sharp objects away, cushion the head with something soft, loosen tight clothing around the neck. Do not move them unless in danger.

steps.title: Do not restrain or put anything in the mouth
steps.detail: Holding limbs can injure them; objects in the mouth break teeth and block the airway. They cannot swallow their tongue.

steps.title: When the jerking stops
steps.detail: Roll them into the recovery position to keep the airway clear. Check breathing. Stay with them, speak calmly and reassure them as they come round; confusion may last 20 minutes or more.

steps.title: Give emergency medication if prescribed and you are trained
steps.detail: Some people carry buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam with a care plan for prolonged seizures.

steps.title: Afterwards
steps.detail: Let them rest. Someone with known epilepsy who recovers fully does not usually need an ambulance.

dont: Do not hold them down or try to stop the movements
Do not put anything in the mouth
Do not give food or drink until fully recovered
Do not leave them alone until fully alert
callFor: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or one seizure after another without recovery
First ever seizure, seizure in water, injury, difficulty breathing after the seizure, or pregnancy
Not regaining consciousness, or the person is known to have diabetes (check glucose)
A febrile seizure in a child lasting more than 5 minutes, or any first febrile seizure
seizures.why: Neurons in the cortex fire in synchronous waves that spread across both hemispheres; the motor cortex drives the stiffening and jerking, and the brainstem's breathing drive is interrupted, which is why lips go blue. Neurons exhaust their energy stores within minutes, ending most seizures; beyond 5 minutes the mechanisms that stop them are failing (status epilepticus) and brain injury becomes likely without drugs that boost GABA inhibition, such as midazolam.

references.title: NHS: What to do if someone has a seizure

heatstroke.name: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
heatstroke.summary: Heat exhaustion is the body struggling to shed heat: sweaty, weak and dizzy, but still thinking clearly, and it recovers with cooling and fluids within 30 minutes. Heatstroke is the failure of that system: core temperature above 40°C with confusion or collapse, which damages the brain, kidneys and muscle and kills without rapid cooling.
recognise: Heat exhaustion: headache, dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, cramps, fast pulse and breathing, temperature 38-40°C, thirst, weakness
Heatstroke: temperature over 40°C, hot skin (may be dry or sweaty), confusion, slurred speech, agitation, seizures, loss of consciousness; fast strong pulse
At risk: babies, older people, athletes and outdoor workers, heart disease, some medicines (diuretics, antipsychotics), alcohol

steps.title: Move to a cool place
steps.detail: Shade, air conditioning or a cool room. Lie them down, raise the feet slightly, remove excess clothing.

steps.title: Cool actively
steps.detail: Spray or sponge with cool water and fan them; cold packs wrapped in cloth to armpits, neck and groin. For a collapsed athlete, immersion in cold water to the neck is the fastest method if it can be done safely.

steps.title: Give fluids if fully alert
steps.detail: Cool water or a sports or rehydration drink, sipped steadily. Nothing by mouth if confused or drowsy.

steps.title: Reassess after 30 minutes
steps.detail: Heat exhaustion should be improving. If they are no better, confused, have a seizure, or stop responding, it is heatstroke: call emergency services and continue cooling until temperature is below 39°C.

steps.title: If unresponsive
steps.detail: Recovery position if breathing; CPR if not.

dont: Do not give paracetamol or aspirin: they do not lower heatstroke temperatures and can harm the liver and kidneys
Do not give alcohol or caffeine
Do not leave anyone in a parked car
Do not wait to see if a confused person improves
callFor: Any confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness or temperature over 40°C
No improvement after 30 minutes of cooling and rest
Heat illness in a baby, young child or frail older adult
heatstroke.why: Muscles and metabolism generate heat that blood carries to the skin, where sweat evaporates to shed it; the hypothalamus runs this thermostat. High humidity stops evaporation, dehydration reduces sweat, and once core temperature passes about 40°C proteins begin to denature: brain cells swell, muscle breaks down (releasing myoglobin that clogs the kidneys), and clotting fails. Cooling the large vessels of the neck, armpits and groin, and evaporative cooling with water and fanning, drop core temperature fastest.

hypothermia.name: Hypothermia and frostbite
hypothermia.summary: Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C. Shivering fails as it deepens, thinking slows, the heart becomes irritable, and below about 28°C it may stop. Gentle handling, insulation and slow rewarming save lives; rough movement can trigger a fatal rhythm. Frostbite is the freezing of tissue itself, usually fingers, toes, nose and ears.
recognise: Mild (32-35°C): shivering, cold pale skin, fast breathing, tiredness, clumsiness, slurred speech
Moderate (28-32°C): shivering stops, confusion, drowsiness, slow shallow breathing, slow weak pulse, may undress ('paradoxical undressing')
Severe (below 28°C): unconscious, barely detectable breathing and pulse, dilated pupils, may appear dead
Frostbite: numb, white or waxy skin that feels hard; blisters and blackening later
At risk: babies, older people, outdoor exposure with wet clothing or wind, alcohol, immersion in cold water, falls at home in a cold house

steps.title: Move to shelter gently
steps.detail: Get them out of wind, rain or water, handling them gently and keeping them horizontal if possible. Call emergency services for anything beyond mild hypothermia.

steps.title: Remove wet clothing and insulate
steps.detail: Replace wet clothes with dry, and wrap in blankets, sleeping bags or foil, including the head; insulate from the ground. Cover but do not rub the skin.

steps.title: Rewarm slowly
steps.detail: Warm the trunk first: body-to-body contact, warm (not hot) packs wrapped in cloth to the chest, armpits and neck. Warm sweet drinks if fully alert and able to swallow.

steps.title: Monitor breathing
steps.detail: Check breathing for up to a minute in severe cases, because it can be very slow. If not breathing, start CPR and continue: people have survived prolonged cold arrests.

steps.title: Frostbite
steps.detail: Remove rings and wet gloves, warm the part against your body or in warm water at about 37-39°C for 30 minutes if there is no risk of refreezing; cover with loose dry dressings between digits, elevate, and seek medical care. Give pain relief; rewarming hurts.

dont: Do not rub or massage the skin, and never rub frostbitten areas with snow
Do not use direct heat (hot water bottles on skin, hot baths, heat lamps), which can cause burns and drives cold blood to the core
Do not give alcohol, which dilates skin vessels and loses heat
Do not assume someone cold and still is dead: 'not dead until warm and dead'
Do not let a frostbitten limb thaw if it may refreeze before reaching care
callFor: Any hypothermia with confusion, drowsiness, or shivering that has stopped
Hypothermia in a baby, an older person, or after cold-water immersion
Frostbite affecting more than the skin surface, or any blistering or blackening
hypothermia.why: Heat is lost by conduction (wet clothes, cold ground), convection (wind) and radiation; the hypothalamus responds with shivering, which quadruples heat production but needs energy. As the core cools, enzymes slow, nerve conduction fails and the heart's conducting system becomes unstable; a jolt can tip an irritable cold heart into ventricular fibrillation. Warming the trunk first and slowly avoids 'afterdrop', where cold blood from the limbs returns to the core. Frozen tissue forms ice crystals that shear cells and clot small vessels.

poisoning.name: Poisoning and overdose
poisoning.summary: A poison is anything taken in a quantity that harms: medicines (paracetamol, opioids, antidepressants), household chemicals, plants, carbon monoxide, alcohol and recreational drugs. Symptoms may be delayed by hours, so the danger cannot be judged by how the person looks. The first-aid tasks are to remove the source, keep the airway safe, and get expert advice quickly with the container in hand.
recognise: Vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, agitation, seizures, unusual breathing (very slow with opioids), small or large pupils
Burns around the mouth with corrosives; a chemical smell; empty packets or bottles
Carbon monoxide: headache, dizziness, nausea, 'flu without fever', in several people in the same building, with gas appliances or engines running indoors
Paracetamol overdose often causes no symptoms for 24 hours, then liver failure

steps.title: Make it safe and get help
steps.detail: Remove them from fumes into fresh air (protect yourself first). Call emergency services if drowsy, breathing abnormally, fitting, or after any deliberate overdose; otherwise call the poisons information line or emergency services for advice.

steps.title: Find out what, how much and when
steps.detail: Keep the container, packets, plant or vomit for identification. Note the time.

steps.title: Swallowed chemicals
steps.detail: Wipe the mouth. Sips of water or milk only if a corrosive was swallowed and they are alert. Do not make them vomit.

steps.title: Chemicals on skin or in eyes
steps.detail: Remove contaminated clothing; flush skin with running water for 20 minutes; rinse an eye with running water for 20 minutes, from the nose outward.

steps.title: Opioid overdose
steps.detail: If breathing is slow or absent with pinpoint pupils, give naloxone if you have it (nasal spray or injection), call emergency services, and support breathing: rescue breaths, or CPR if no normal breathing.

steps.title: Unconscious but breathing
steps.detail: Recovery position; monitor breathing continuously as it can stop. Not breathing: CPR (use a face shield for rescue breaths if chemicals are involved).

dont: Do not induce vomiting: corrosives burn twice and vomit can enter the lungs
Do not give anything to eat or drink unless advised (except sips of water for corrosives)
Do not assume a person who took paracetamol and feels fine is safe: treatment must start within 8 hours to be fully effective
Do not leave them alone, and do not let them 'sleep it off' after an overdose
callFor: Any deliberate overdose, any child who has swallowed medicine or chemicals, any opioid overdose
Drowsiness, abnormal breathing, seizures, chest pain, or suspected carbon monoxide
Any paracetamol overdose, even without symptoms
poisoning.why: Most poisons are absorbed through the small intestine and processed by the liver; paracetamol overwhelms the liver's glutathione and its toxic metabolite kills liver cells over days, which acetylcysteine prevents if given early. Opioids act on the brainstem's breathing centre; naloxone displaces them from the receptors within minutes but wears off before the opioid does. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin 200 times more tightly than oxygen, starving tissues while the oximeter reads falsely normal.

allergic-reactions.name: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)
allergic-reactions.summary: Anaphylaxis is a whole-body allergic reaction, usually within minutes of a food, sting or drug, in which mast cells flood the body with histamine and other mediators: airways swell and tighten, vessels leak and dilate, and blood pressure collapses. Adrenaline injected into the thigh muscle reverses all of these and is the only treatment that works; antihistamines and inhalers are not enough.
recognise: Airway: swelling of the tongue, lips or throat, hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing
Breathing: wheeze, tight chest, noisy or fast breathing, persistent cough
Circulation: pale, clammy, faint, dizzy, collapse, confusion, fast weak pulse
Often with itching, hives, flushing, swelling of the face, stomach cramps or vomiting; but skin signs are absent in a fifth of cases
Triggers: nuts, milk, egg, shellfish, wasp and bee stings, penicillin and other drugs, latex

steps.title: Use the adrenaline auto-injector at once
steps.detail: Any airway, breathing or circulation problem after an exposure means anaphylaxis. Remove the safety cap, press the tip firmly into the outer mid-thigh (through clothing if needed) and hold for the device's count (3-10 seconds). Note the time.

steps.title: Call emergency services
steps.detail: Say 'anaphylaxis'. Do this even if they improve: reactions can return hours later.

steps.title: Position
steps.detail: Lie them flat with legs raised if faint or dizzy; sit up if breathing is the main problem; on their side if vomiting or unconscious. Do not let them stand or walk, even to reach help: sudden standing can cause cardiac arrest.

steps.title: Second dose
steps.detail: If no improvement after 5 minutes, give a second auto-injector if available.

steps.title: Remove the trigger if possible
steps.detail: Flick out a bee sting with a card edge; stop any drug infusion.

steps.title: If they stop breathing normally
steps.detail: Start CPR.

dont: Do not wait for skin symptoms or for it to get worse before using adrenaline
Do not rely on antihistamine tablets or an asthma inhaler for anaphylaxis
Do not let the person stand up or walk
Do not inject adrenaline into a finger or vein
callFor: Every case of suspected anaphylaxis, whether or not adrenaline has been given, for observation of 6-12 hours
Any allergic reaction with breathing difficulty, swelling of the mouth or throat, or faintness
allergic-reactions.why: IgE antibodies on mast cells recognise the allergen and trigger degranulation within minutes. Histamine and leukotrienes constrict bronchial smooth muscle (wheeze), swell the tongue and larynx (the narrowest part of the airway), and open capillaries so plasma pours into tissues while arteries dilate, dropping blood pressure. Adrenaline acts on alpha receptors to constrict vessels and reduce swelling, and on beta receptors to open airways, strengthen the heart and stop further mast-cell release. The thigh's vastus lateralis has a rich blood supply for fast absorption.

electric-shock.name: Electric shock
electric-shock.summary: Electricity passing through the body can stop the heart, paralyse breathing muscles, burn tissue along its path far more deeply than the skin marks suggest, and throw the person against objects. The first rule is not to become the second casualty: break contact safely before touching them.
recognise: Person in contact with a live source, unable to let go, or found collapsed near one
Burns at the entry and exit points (often hand and foot), which may look small
Unconsciousness, absent or abnormal breathing, irregular pulse
Muscle pain, numbness, confusion, seizures; injuries from falls or being thrown
Lightning: linear or feathery burns, ruptured eardrums, temporary paralysis

steps.title: Make it safe
steps.detail: Low voltage (household): switch off at the mains or unplug. If you cannot, stand on dry insulating material and push them clear with a wooden broom or chair; do not touch them directly. High voltage (power lines, railways, substations): stay at least 18 metres away and call emergency services; do not approach until the supply is confirmed off.

steps.title: Call emergency services
steps.detail: For any shock beyond a minor tingle, and always for loss of consciousness, burns, or a high-voltage or lightning injury.

steps.title: Check response and breathing
steps.detail: If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and send for a defibrillator; electrical cardiac arrests respond well to defibrillation.

steps.title: Treat burns
steps.detail: Cool entry and exit burns with running water for 20 minutes and cover loosely. Look for both points.

steps.title: Treat other injuries
steps.detail: Suspect spinal injury if thrown; keep them still. Treat for shock: lie down, keep warm, nothing by mouth.

dont: Do not touch someone still in contact with electricity
Do not use anything wet or metal to move them
Do not approach high-voltage sources or a downed cable
Do not assume a small skin burn means a small injury
callFor: Any electric shock with unconsciousness, burns, chest pain, palpitations, breathing difficulty, or in pregnancy
All high-voltage and lightning injuries
Any shock in a child, or any household shock that caused more than a brief tingle (heart rhythm monitoring may be needed)
electric-shock.why: Current follows the path of least resistance through wet, conductive tissues: blood vessels, nerves and muscle. Alternating current at mains frequency causes muscles to contract and hold on, and if the path crosses the chest it can throw the heart into ventricular fibrillation or stop the diaphragm. Heat generated along the path cooks deep tissue, and muscle breakdown can clog the kidneys. Lightning is a direct-current flashover that more often causes cardiac and respiratory arrest than deep burns.

wound-care.name: Cuts, grazes and wound care
wound-care.summary: Most cuts and grazes heal on their own if they are cleaned, closed and kept covered. The aims are to stop bleeding, remove dirt and bacteria, bring the edges together so new skin can bridge the gap, and spot the wounds that need stitches, antibiotics or a tetanus booster.
recognise: Graze: surface skin scraped off, oozing, dirty
Cut (laceration or incision): edges may gape; bleeding depends on depth and site (scalp and face bleed freely)
Puncture: small entry, deep track, high infection risk (nails, bites, splinters)
Infection developing days later: spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, increasing pain, fever, red streaks up the limb

steps.title: Wash your hands and stop the bleeding
steps.detail: Apply pressure with a clean cloth for 10 minutes; raise the part above the heart.

steps.title: Clean the wound
steps.detail: Rinse under running tap water for several minutes to flush out dirt. Pat dry with a clean towel. Remove loose grit with clean tweezers; leave anything deeply embedded for a clinician.

steps.title: Close and cover
steps.detail: Bring the edges of a small cut together with adhesive strips. Cover with a sterile non-stick dressing or plaster; change it daily or if wet or dirty. Keep it covered until healed.

steps.title: Pain relief
steps.detail: Paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed.

steps.title: Watch for infection
steps.detail: Check daily. Seek care for spreading redness, pus, increasing pain or fever.

dont: Do not use antiseptic solutions, hydrogen peroxide or iodine inside a wound: they damage healing tissue; tap water is best
Do not pull out deeply embedded objects
Do not close dirty wounds, bites or wounds more than 12-24 hours old with strips or glue: they need cleaning and often antibiotics
Do not pick scabs
callFor: Bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure, or spurting blood
A wound that gapes, is longer than about 2 cm, is on the face, over a joint or on the hand with loss of movement or sensation (may need stitches within 12-24 hours)
Animal or human bites, deep puncture wounds, wounds contaminated with soil or glass, or something embedded
Signs of infection, or a tetanus vaccination more than 10 years ago (5 for dirty wounds)
wound-care.why: The skin's epidermis regrows from the edges and from hair follicles at about a millimetre a day; the dermis beneath rebuilds with collagen, which is why deep cuts scar. Keeping a wound moist and covered speeds cell migration, and closing the edges shortens the distance new skin must cross. Bacteria in soil and animal mouths (Clostridium tetani, Pasteurella) thrive in deep, oxygen-poor puncture tracks, which is why those wounds are cleaned open and given antibiotics rather than sealed.
